title: Wellbeing, vulnerability and resilience
blurb: Notice when you or a colleague are struggling, act in a way that is kind and safe, and use restorative supervision and self-care to stay well in a demanding job.
question: A week after a difficult stillbirth, a midwife notices her colleague is tearful, withdrawn and has made two small documentation errors. What is the most appropriate first response?

teach.h: Looking after the people who give care
teach.body: SPM 5.14 asks midwives to recognise signs of vulnerability in themselves or colleagues and act to minimise risks to health and wellbeing. SPM 5.15 asks them to manage the personal and emotional challenges of work, workload, uncertainty and change, and to practise compassionate self-care. Code 20.9 requires you to maintain the level of health you need for your role. In plain English: you cannot pour from an empty cup, and noticing a struggling colleague is part of keeping women safe.

teach.caption: Signs to notice, not a diagnosis. Ask kindly and privately.

root.label: A colleague is struggling
root.sub: Code 8.7: support, never at the expense of safety

children.label: Tell the person in charge now

teach.body: A-EQUIP (advocating and educating for quality improvement) is NHS England's model of clinical midwifery supervision, delivered by Professional Midwifery Advocates (PMAs). Its restorative function has been shown to reduce stress and burnout, improve retention, job satisfaction, working relationships and work–life balance. Providers must make sure every midwife has the opportunity to meet a PMA at least once a year, and the PMA should be available as the need arises.

Anna cared for a woman whose baby was stillborn. A week later her colleague Ife notices she is tearful, quiet, and has made two small documentation errors. Ife finds a private moment, says what she has noticed and asks how Anna is. Anna admits she is not sleeping. Ife listens, suggests a session with the PMA and the trust's staff support service, and offers to check in later. There is no immediate risk, so supportive steps come first.

head: Staff indicator
Why it matters
teach.caption: NICE NG4 Box 4. NBCP standard 9 also asks for staff wellbeing to be prioritised with a trauma-informed approach.

rows.label: Take your breaks and report when you cannot
Use restorative supervision after hard events
Tell someone in authority early if you cannot cope
Build on what you and the team do well

teach.text: Being unwell or off sick does not in itself mean your fitness to practise is impaired. But kindness to a colleague is not secrecy about a risk: if someone is unsafe right now, the person in charge must know.

items: Code 20.9: maintain the health you need for your role; Code 16.3: tell someone in authority early if problems may stop you working within the Code.
Notice signs of vulnerability in yourself and colleagues (SPM 5.14) and ask privately and kindly.
Support colleagues, but never at the expense of safety (Code 8.7).
A-EQUIP restorative supervision with a PMA reduces stress and burnout; every midwife can meet a PMA at least yearly.
Missed breaks, overtime, sickness and morale are NG4 staffing indicators.

summary: You can now recognise when you or a colleague are vulnerable and respond in a way that is both kind and safe. You can also use restorative supervision, staff support and compassionate self-care to manage workload, uncertainty and change.

A.q: Which NMC Code standard requires midwives to maintain the level of health they need to carry out their role?
options: Code 20.9
Code 8.7
Code 13.3
Code 22.3
A.why: Code 20.9: maintain the level of health you need to carry out your professional role.

whyNot.1: Code 8.7 is about supporting colleagues with health or performance problems.
whyNot.2: Code 13.3 is about asking for help beyond your competence.
whyNot.3: Code 22.3 is about keeping knowledge and skills up to date.

A.q: Which function of the A-EQUIP model is mainly concerned with midwives' wellbeing and reducing burnout?
options: Normative
Formative
Restorative
Personal action for quality improvement
A.why: The restorative function (clinical supervision) supports wellbeing and has been shown to reduce stress and burnout.

whyNot.0: Normative concerns monitoring, evaluation and quality control.
whyNot.3: Personal action for QI concerns contributing to quality improvement.

A.q: A colleague has been tearful and withdrawn since a difficult birth and has made two small documentation errors. What is the best first response?
options: Report her errors to the manager in writing
Speak to her privately and ask how she is
Check all her notes for further errors
Suggest she takes annual leave next week
A.why: SPM 5.14: recognise signs of vulnerability and act. With no immediate risk, a private, compassionate conversation and signposting to support come first.

whyNot.0: A formal report first is unkind and may stop her seeking help; small errors can be corrected with her.
whyNot.2: Auditing her notes without speaking to her misses the cause.
whyNot.3: Leave may help, but first find out how she is and what support she needs.

B.q: A midwife has worked extra shifts for weeks, feels exhausted and has nearly made a medicine error. What should she do?
options: Keep going until the staffing improves
Take a day off without telling anyone
Tell her manager early and seek support
Report herself to the NMC
B.why: Code 16.3 and 20.9: tell someone in authority at the first reasonable opportunity if problems may stop you working within the Code, and look after your health.

whyNot.0: Continuing while exhausted increases the risk to women and herself.
whyNot.1: Unplanned absence without telling anyone leaves the service unsafe.
whyNot.3: Exhaustion is managed through support at work, not a self-referral.

B.q: Midwives on a postnatal ward regularly miss their breaks. Under NICE NG4, how should this be treated?
options: As a personal choice for each midwife
As acceptable on busy shifts
As a disciplinary matter for the team
As a staffing indicator to record and review
B.why: NG4 Box 4 lists missed breaks as a staff-reported safe midwifery staffing indicator to record and review.

whyNot.0: Missed breaks reflect workload, not choice.
whyNot.1: Accepting them as normal hides a safety signal.
whyNot.2: Missed breaks signal a staffing problem, not misconduct.

B.q: A midwife is returning to work after sick leave for anxiety. She asks whether she must tell the NMC her fitness to practise is impaired. What is the correct position?
options: Yes, any mental illness must be declared
Yes, if she was off for more than 3 months
No, sick leave alone does not mean impairment
No, health is not a fitness to practise matter
B.why: NMC guidance: being signed off sick, or having a disability or long-term condition, does not necessarily mean fitness to practise is impaired; the NMC acts where there is a risk of harm.

whyNot.0: There is no rule that every mental illness must be declared as impairment.
whyNot.1: There is no 3-month threshold for impairment.
whyNot.3: Health can be an FtP issue where it creates a risk to the public.

C.q: A colleague confides she is struggling with burnout and asks you to tell no one. She is working safely. What is the best response?
options: Report her burnout to the manager today
Keep her secret and not raise it again
Suggest she moves to a less busy unit
Encourage support and agree next steps
C.why: With no immediate risk, respect her trust while encouraging support (PMA, occupational health, GP) and agreeing a plan; if she becomes unsafe, Code 8.7 requires action.

whyNot.0: With no immediate risk, overriding her confidence first may stop her seeking help.
whyNot.1: Saying nothing at all leaves her without support.
whyNot.2: Moving her away is not a supportive or proportionate response.

C.q: After a neonatal death, the labour ward team is distressed. Which response from the unit best reflects NBCP standard 9?
options: Offer trauma-informed support and wellbeing services
Expect staff to carry on as normal
Arrange extra bereavement care training for all staff
Move the staff involved to another area
C.why: NBCP standard 9: staff wellbeing is prioritised and monitored, with a trauma-informed approach and access to wellbeing services.

whyNot.1: Expecting staff to carry on ignores their needs.
whyNot.2: Training is standard 8, not the support standard.
whyNot.3: Moving staff does not provide support.

C.q: A midwife feels anxious about a planned reorganisation of community teams. Which response best reflects SPM 5.15?
options: Avoid thinking about it until it happens
Use supervision and seek clear information
Resist the changes through informal complaints
Look for a job in another trust
C.why: SPM 5.15: manage the personal and emotional challenges of change; supervision and accurate information help, and concerns can be raised through proper channels.

whyNot.0: Avoidance does not manage the challenge.
whyNot.2: Informal complaints are not a constructive route to influence change.
whyNot.3: Leaving avoids rather than manages the challenge.

reteach.title: Notice, ask, support, escalate if unsafe
reteach.question: What do you do when a colleague is not themselves?

blocks.body: Notice the signs: tiredness, withdrawal, small errors, skipped breaks. Ask privately and kindly. Support: listen and signpost restorative supervision with a PMA, staff support or occupational health. Escalate if unsafe: if she is a risk to women or babies right now, the person in charge must know, while you stay kind.

blocks.text: Support first when there is no immediate risk; safety first when there is.

explain.body: A-EQUIP cites reductions in stress and burnout, better job satisfaction and retention, improved working relationships, and better work–life balance.

test.q: Which outcome has restorative clinical supervision been shown to improve?
options: Caesarean birth rates
Booking times
Breastfeeding rates
Staff retention
test.why: A-EQUIP cites evidence that the restorative function improves retention and reduces stress and burnout.

whyNot.0: Caesarean rates are not a cited outcome of restorative supervision.
whyNot.1: Booking times are not a cited outcome.
whyNot.2: Breastfeeding rates are not a cited outcome.

explain.body: Providers must ensure all midwives have the opportunity to meet a PMA at least once a year if required, and the PMA is available as the need arises.

test.q: Under A-EQUIP, how often must every midwife have the opportunity to meet a Professional Midwifery Advocate, as a minimum?
options: At least once a month
At least every 3 months
At least once a year
At least every 3 years
test.why: Providers must ensure all midwives can meet a PMA at least once a year, more often if needed.

whyNot.0: Monthly is not the minimum set; frequency depends on need.
whyNot.1: Three-monthly is not the minimum set.
whyNot.3: Three years is the revalidation cycle.

explain.body: SPM 5.13.5: build resilience by noticing and using strengths: what you did well, the skills in your team, and what helped in hard situations.

test.q: Which question best reflects a strength-based approach in a team debrief?
options: Who was responsible for the delay?
What helped us manage this well?
Why did nobody follow the protocol?
How many errors were made?
test.why: A strength-based approach looks for what helped and builds on it.

whyNot.0: Seeking a responsible person is a blame focus.
whyNot.2: This focuses on failure rather than strengths.
whyNot.3: Counting errors is a deficit focus.

explain.body: Code 8.7: be supportive of colleagues encountering health or performance problems, but this support must never compromise or be at the expense of patient or public safety.

test.q: A colleague who is clearly unwell asks you to cover for her so she can stay on shift caring for a woman in labour. What should you do?
options: Tell the person in charge
Cover her tasks quietly
Advise her to rest in the staff room
Ask the woman whether she minds
test.why: Code 8.7: support her, but not at the expense of safety; the person in charge needs to know so care can be reallocated.

whyNot.2: Resting does not arrange safe care for the woman.
whyNot.3: The woman should not be asked to manage a staffing risk.
